display: Salvador & Baía de Todos os Santos
tagline: Brazil's largest bay already moves 7.5 million people a year across the water — a regulated ferry-and-lancha habit, a car-free resort island 38 nm south, and a 2.9-million-person metro on the shore, all waiting to fly.
summary: Salvador sits on the Baía de Todos os Santos, Brazil's biggest bay, and water transport here is not a proposal — it is a daily habit regulated by the state agency AGERBA. The São Joaquim–Bom Despacho ferry and the Salvador–Mar Grande lanchas carried 7.49 million passengers in 2025, and premium catamarans run three-plus times a day to car-free Morro de São Paulo, 2h30 away with 90 minutes of open-Atlantic swell. The bay is dotted with destination islands — Blue Flag Ilha dos Frades, historic Itaparica, artisanal Ilha de Maré — served today by slow diesel schooners and lanchas. A foiling-electric layer modernizes an adopted habit: smoother than the swell, quieter than the schooners, faster than everything on the water today.

use_cases.title: Fly the crossing millions already make
use_cases.body: Foot-passenger foiling shuttles overlaid on the two regulated crossings — São Joaquim–Bom Despacho (~7 nm, hourly ferry taking 60–80 minutes today) and Terminal Náutico–Mar Grande (~6 nm lanchas every 30 minutes). Cut the crossing to ~20 minutes, absorb Carnival and summer surges, and give AGERBA a clean-fleet story during the bridge-construction years.

use_cases.title: The Morro de São Paulo flagship
use_cases.body: A ~38 nm foiling service from the Terminal Náutico to car-free Morro de São Paulo, flying above the open-Atlantic swell that makes today's 2h30 catamaran a seasickness run. Faster, smoother, and silent on arrival at the island's pier — with Boipeba one 15 nm hop further south.

use_cases.title: Bay-of-all-Saints island spider
use_cases.body: Premium foiling day-charters from Bahia Marina and the Yacht Clube da Bahia across the bay's islands — Blue Flag Ilha dos Frades (~13 nm), historic Itaparica town (~12 nm), Ilha de Maré — replacing the diesel schooner fleet with silent zero-wake hops between beaches.

use_cases.title: Northern-bay commute spurs
use_cases.body: Sheltered-water links from Marina Aratu and São Tomé de Paripe to the city-centre waterfront (~12 nm), serving the Aratu industrial belt and the bridge-construction workforce, plus the no-bridge community crossing to Ilha de Maré.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire Baía de Todos os Santos mesh sits deep inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope: Mar Grande (~6 nm), Bom Despacho (~7 nm), Ilha dos Frades (~13 nm), Itaparica town (~12 nm), Aratu (~12 nm), Ilha de Maré (~2.5 nm) — sheltered bay water, marina charging at Bahia Marina and Marina Itaparica, and zero-wake operation around protected mangrove shores. Even the marquee Morro de São Paulo run (~38 nm) and its Boipeba extension (~50 nm from Salvador) fit the electric envelope with fast-charge turnarounds.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range extends the network beyond the bay with no charging-infrastructure dependency — south past Boipeba to the Camamu bay and Península de Maraú (~65–70 nm), onward to Ilhéus (~120 nm), and north up the Costa dos Coqueiros toward Praia do Forte — turning the whole Bahian coast into one connected water corridor anchored on Salvador.

competitive_landscape: Water mobility here is a functioning, regulated market — the strongest possible demand evidence. Internacional Travessias runs the São Joaquim–Bom Despacho ferry-boat hourly with vessels up to 987 passengers; a lancha service crosses to Mar Grande every 30 minutes from the Terminal Náutico (managed by Socicam); several catamaran operators run 3+ daily departures to Morro de São Paulo; and a schooner fleet works the island day-tour circuit. The pain is equally documented: 60–80 minute ferry crossings, holiday queues tracked by a live 'filômetro', an ageing fleet the state is actively renewing (a new R$89.4M, 1,254-passenger ferry was contracted in May 2026), and a seasickness-prone open-water leg on the marquee tourist route. Every one of those pains is a foiling-electric upgrade path, not a new market to invent.
seasonality: Peak is the austral summer, December–March: the Verão de Salvador season (≈2.8M tourists), Réveillon and Carnival, when AGERBA mounts special ferry operations (~300k pedestrians in Carnival 2026 alone). June brings São João holiday surges. Winter (May–August) is the rainy season with a long dry, mild shoulder from September. The inner bay is sheltered year-round — ideal electric-foiling water — while the exposed Atlantic leg to Morro de São Paulo picks up southeast trade swell, which is precisely where a foiling hull's above-the-wave ride beats every conventional catamaran. Humpback whale season (July–November) adds a shoulder-season tourism draw on the southern routes. No cyclone exposure.
regulatory_note: A single state regulator, AGERBA, governs the ferry-boat system, the Salvador–Mar Grande lancha crossing and the Salvador–Morro de São Paulo travessia, setting tariffs by published resolution (latest: Resolução Nº 11, March 2026) — one authority relationship covers the three biggest corridors. Vessel classification and crewing sit with the Brazilian Navy (Capitania dos Portos da Bahia); the Terminal Náutico is professionally managed under Socicam. Timing matters: the state is investing in fleet renewal now, and the R$11.6bn Salvador–Itaparica bridge (35-year concession, under construction) will reshape the vehicle crossing over several years — leaving fast, clean foot-passenger and island services as the water network's growth story, with the state publicly committed to protecting the bay environment as the island economy grows.

precedents.why_it_matters: Proof that electric foiling can be the backbone of an island-mobility network at national scale — the same pattern as Salvador's bay: one hub city, many boat-only islands, tourism and daily transit on the same water.

precedents.what: State-regulated water transit with published tariffs and live queue telemetry
precedents.why_it_matters: A mature regulatory framework — tariff resolutions, concession structure, special-operation planning — means a clean-fleet service can plug into existing rules rather than pioneering them.
